record.original_question: For n terminals, consider full Steiner topologies, meaning the underlying abstract graphs of full Steiner trees. How many different full Steiner topologies may simultaneously give a shortest solution to the Steiner problem for the same terminal set?

evidence.quote:
Question 2.12. It is known, see [17], that the total number of full Steiner topologies (the underlying abstract graphs) with
n terminals is
(2n − 4)!
2
n−2(n − 2)!.
How many of them may simultaneously give a shortest solution to the Steiner problem?

In all known examples the number is at most exponential in n while the number of topologies has a factorial order of
growth. Note that the answer may depend heavily on the dimension.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A Steiner tree for a finite terminal set $T = \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\}$ in Euclidean space (or, more generally, in a fixed metric space) is a finite tree whose vertex set contains $T$ and whose remaining vertices, called Steiner points, are auxiliary; the tree's length is the sum of the lengths of its edges. A Steiner tree is called full if every terminal is a leaf (degree 1) and every Steiner point has degree at least 3 (in the Euclidean case, exactly 3). The full Steiner topology of a full Steiner tree is the underlying abstract (combinatorial) tree, regarded up to isomorphism that fixes the labeling of terminals. The total number of distinct full Steiner topologies on $n$ labeled terminals equals
$$\frac{(2n-4)!}{2^{\,n-2}(n-2)!}.$$
A shortest (minimal) Steiner tree for $T$ is one of minimum total length among all Steiner trees connecting $T$. Define
$$f(n) := \max_{T} \#\bigl\{\text{distinct full Steiner topologies realized by some shortest full Steiner tree on } T\bigr\},$$
where the maximum is taken over all $n$-element terminal sets (in a given ambient space, e.g.\ the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, or $\mathbb{R}^d$ for fixed $d$).

Determine $f(n)$, or at least its order of growth as $n \to \infty$. In particular, can $f(n)$ ever be of factorial order, matching the total count $(2n-4)!/(2^{n-2}(n-2)!)$, or is it bounded by an exponential function of $n$? How does the answer depend on the ambient dimension $d$?
artifact.status_search_result: No source was found that determines the maximum number of full Steiner topologies that can simultaneously be realized by shortest Steiner trees on a common terminal set. Standard references on the Steiner tree problem state only the total count $(2n-4)!/(2^{n-2}(n-2)!)$ of full topologies and discuss enumeration and uniqueness of optima in special cases, but no general formula or matching upper/lower bound on the multiplicity of minimizing topologies appears in the literature consulted. The problem appears open, with known examples giving at most exponential multiplicity.

status_evidence.title: On the History of the Euclidean Steiner Tree Problem
status_evidence.snippet: Counts the number of full Steiner topologies via the double-factorial formula, but does not address how many can simultaneously be optimal.
status_evidence.claim: Standard reference giving the total count of full Steiner topologies but not the multiplicity of minimizers.

status_evidence.title: Minimum Steiner Tree Construction (Robins–Zelikovsky)
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of Steiner minimal tree theory and algorithms; discusses topology enumeration without giving a bound on the number of co-optimal full topologies for a single terminal set.
status_evidence.claim: No bound on simultaneously minimizing full topologies is stated.
